## TL;DR

Ran a mobile-width QA pass over RepoOS login, OTP, expired-session routing, sign-out, and the Hub return-to-picker path. The OTP error was visible but was not announced to assistive technology, and all three auth inputs depended on placeholders for their names. I added live alert semantics to both login error displays and explicit accessible names to the administrator email, sign-in email, and one-time-code fields. At 375px, the login card and OTP controls fit without horizontal overflow. The focused regression suite passed: 34 tests across the new login accessibility test and the existing router and Hub return tests.

## Work and rationale

The task calls for a phone-width pass through login, code entry, expired sessions, sign-out, and pairing. I read the task instructions first and kept all implementation and QA work in this task worktree. I did not modify `repoos.toml`, inspect or edit the main checkout, or use a visible browser. The requested QA server is auth-less, so it does not expose the normal authenticated login path by itself. To exercise the auth screen against that server without accessing an account or email provider, I used headless WebKit and intercepted only the auth status and OTP endpoints in Playwright.

At a 375 × 844 CSS-pixel viewport, the login card was 327px wide, began 24px from the viewport edge, and had no horizontal overflow. In OTP entry, the action row fit inside its 273px content width. I submitted an invalid/expired code and confirmed the UI displayed “Invalid or expired code.” The message was visually clear, but rendered as an ordinary paragraph without announcement semantics. I gave both bootstrap and sign-in errors `role="alert"` so assistive technology receives newly displayed errors. I also added explicit accessible names to the three inputs in the bootstrap, email, and OTP steps. Placeholders remain examples; they are no longer the only source of each field’s name.

The separate sign-out pass opened the user menu at 375px, submitted logout through an intercepted endpoint, and observed navigation to `/login`. The app stayed within the viewport. Since the backing server was configured to disable auth, the pass supplied mocked responses for status, current-user, and logout. Dashboard startup also attempted other protected data requests; those generated expected access-control noise in the auth-less setup and did not interfere with the logout assertion.

The task’s “pairing” flow maps to native Hub WebView return-to-picker behavior in this codebase, not a separate web pairing form. Existing Hub return tests exercise token and origin checks, preserving Hub context through a login round-trip, showing the return affordance on the login screen, and closing the native browser only for the valid return navigation. This run did not involve a physical device, so the report does not claim device verification.

I added a focused regression test that checks the rendered source contract for named auth fields and live alerts. Together with the existing router-guard and Hub return test files, the focused run passed all 34 tests. The browser checks were run headlessly against the auth-less server started from this task worktree.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected the login component, auth route handlers, router guard, auth store, top-bar logout control, Hub shell return logic, and existing auth and mobile QA tests. I used the project’s existing QA report style to structure the measurement and evidence. For browser coverage, I tried starting the long-running server in a standalone tool session; the runner reclaimed that helper before the browser connected. I then ran the server and Playwright in the same process group, with a unique port after discovering another concurrent QA task occupied the default port. The successful pass exercised login and OTP states with mocked auth responses and a separate sign-out interaction.

## Challenges and blockers

The auth-less server’s configuration prevents direct login, OTP delivery, and session issuance. Mocking the auth endpoints allowed the browser to inspect those screens while preserving the task’s server requirement, but it is not evidence of a production email delivery or real account login. The Hub pairing return action requires a native WebView to observe the final browser dismissal; only its web contract and login affordance were covered by existing automated tests. No physical device was available or used. There were no code or test blockers for the changes made.

## Key learnings

At a narrow width, the existing login card and OTP controls already fit comfortably; changing their layout would have been unnecessary. The more consequential issue was that a visible server error did not communicate its arrival to assistive technology, and placeholder text alone did not provide a persistent accessible name. A small semantic change addressed both without changing the current visual design or flow. For this task, auth-less server verification works best when Playwright intercepts only the auth calls it needs and leaves the remaining app server requests untouched. The resulting report distinguishes mocked screen behavior and automated Hub contract coverage from real email or device evidence.
